papers.title: Learning-Augmented Coordination Mechanisms
papers.abstract: The inefficiency of decentralized resource allocation is classically measured by the Price of Anarchy (PoA) and the Price of Stability (PoS). The most widely studied and foundational class of these models are atomic and non-atomic congestion games, for which a robust theory quantifying the inefficiency of equilibria is well-established. To mitigate the effects of selfish behavior, we employ Coordination Mechanisms, which modify resource costs to incentivize socially improved equilibria. However, standard Coordination Mechanisms assume unknown, adversarial demand, restricting positive results mainly to specialized networks such as parallel links. We address this limitation by studying learning-augmented coordination mechanisms, where the mechanism is endowed with a potentially inaccurate prediction of the demand. We study general atomic and non-atomic congestion games with polynomial latency functions of degree $d$. Our main positive result is a learning-augmented coordination mechanism tuned by a confidence parameter $β$ which achieves a "best of both worlds" type of result: approximately optimal performance for an accurate prediction without sacrificing the worst-case guarantee of a good equilibrium (PoS). We further establish bounds on PoA-Robustness (worst equilibrium performance under cost modification). Our construction relies on transforming approximate equilibria of the original game into exact equilibria of the modified game using an approximate potential function. We complement our positive results with impossibility results. We first show that requiring all equilibria to have optimal social cost under an accurate prediction precludes bounded robustness. We also show a strong error tolerance limit in non-atomic games: even infinitesimal prediction errors can cause the performance of a mechanism with optimal consistency to revert to the original PoA.

papers.title: Tight Characterizations of AMM Mechanism Design under Weak Efficiency
papers.abstract: Miner extractable value (MEV) poses a persistent challenge for blockchain ecosystems. It arises from the fact that a block builder can exploit its unilateral control over transaction inclusion and ordering to extract profit, potentially at users' expense. Recent work has explored consensus-aided mechanism design to mitigate MEV. This approach combines generic consensus-layer guarantees with application-layer mechanisms that use these guarantees to address application-specific MEV problems. Prior work exemplifies this approach for automated market makers (AMMs). When the consensus layer offers fair sequencing, which orders transactions according to their arrival times, their proposed mechanism achieves incentive compatibility (IC) and weak local efficiency (wLE). Informally, IC rules out profitable strategic deviations by users and builders. Meanwhile, wLE ensures that after execution, any order willing to trade at the initial price cannot benefit from further trade with the pool at the ending marginal price. In this work, we resolve the main open question left by prior works: whether IC and wLE can be achieved under plain consensus (e.g., current Ethereum) without fair sequencing. We prove that no deterministic, anonymous batch AMM can achieve both properties. The impossibility holds even when the consensus layer guarantees censorship resilience and block space is unlimited, establishing the first separation between censorship resilience and fair sequencing in the context of decentralized mechanism design. Our impossibility proof combines three strategic capabilities: creating Sybil identities, over-reporting budgets, and misreporting values. We further show the tightness of our impossibility result: removing any one from the strategy space restores feasibility under censorship resilience. Specifically, we construct a mechanism achieving IC and wLE for each restricted setting.

papers.title: An Unconditional Space-Approximation Lower Bound for Semi-Streaming Matching
papers.abstract: We prove the first unconditional lower bound tradeoff between the number of passes and the approximation factor of maximum matchings in the semi-streaming model. Specifically, we show that any algorithm that outputs an $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximation to maximum matching requires $Ω(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ passes for constant $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$. Prior to our result, such tradeoffs were proven only conditioned on a certain combinatorial assumption about the density of Ruzsa-Szemerédi graphs. The state-of-the-art unconditional lower bound rules out any approximation factor better than $(8/9)$ in two passes but leaves open the possibility of a $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximation for any $\varepsilon > 0$ even in three passes. We provide two different proofs of our result: the first proof uses the recent hierarchical-embedding framework of Assadi, Konrad, Naidu, and Sundaresan (STOC 2024) along with combinatorial constructions using Ruzsa-Szemerédi graphs. The second extends the two-level Ruzsa-Szemerédi hierarchy of Konrad and Naidu (SODA 2024) beyond two levels and proves the corresponding communication lower bound directly by induction, rather than through a reduction to Index.

papers.title: Uniformity Testing for the Monomer-Dimer Model
papers.abstract: We study uniformity testing for the monomer-dimer model on a known graph $G=(V,E)$. Given samples from an unknown distribution $D_w(M)\propto \prod_{e\in M} w_e$ over matchings $M$ of $G$, we ask whether $D_w$ is the uniform distribution over all matchings of $G$ or is $\varepsilon$-far from it in total variation distance. Our main result is that, for every maximum-degree bound $Δ$, uniformity can be tested with $\widetilde O_Δ(\sqrt m/\varepsilon^2)$ samples, where $m=|E|$. We complement this with an information-theoretic lower bound for general graphs: for every pair of parameters $n\le m\le n^2$, there are graphs with $Θ(n)$ vertices and $Θ(m)$ edges on which every tester requires $Ω(\sqrt m/\varepsilon^2)$ samples. Thus, for bounded-degree graph families with $m=Θ(n)$, testing uniformity over the space of matchings has $\widetilde Θ(\sqrt n/\varepsilon^2)$ sample complexity, in contrast with the $Θ(n/\varepsilon^2)$ samples needed to estimate $D_w$ in total variation distance.

papers.title: Sybil-Proofness of Generalized Adaptive Clinching and Implications for Blockchain Mechanism Design
papers.abstract: The adaptive clinching auction of Dobzinski, Lavi, and Nisan (FOCS'08) is a cornerstone of mechanism design with budget-constrained bidders, and it has since inspired a broad range of extensions to substantially richer market settings. Adaptive clinching enjoys compelling guarantees: it is Pareto optimal, and truthful bidding is a dominant strategy whenever budgets cannot be overreported. In many real-world environments, however, identities are cheap to create, making resilience to Sybil attacks an additional requirement. Whether the guarantees of adaptive clinching survive when a bidder can split its budget across fake identities has remained open. We introduce a generalized framework for adaptive clinching and prove that it satisfies Sybil-robust incentive compatibility: a bidder cannot benefit from splitting into any finite number of identities with arbitrary value reports, provided their aggregate reported budget does not exceed the bidder's enforceable true budget. Sybil resilience thus joins the list of ideal properties of adaptive clinching. Our work is motivated by practical problems in decentralized finance, where automated market makers (AMMs) are among the most widely used applications. We design a new AMM mechanism that extends classical adaptive clinching in two ways: it supports a two-sided market and protects against two-sided strategies, and it allows the supply function to depend on the auction state. Its one-sided special case is captured by our generalized adaptive clinching framework, and our proof techniques show that the full two-sided mechanism simultaneously satisfies Sybil-robust incentive compatibility and a relaxed notion of Pareto optimality. We argue that these guarantees are essentially the best possible via impossibility results. More broadly, our work reveals new connections between classical algorithmic game theory and modern decentralized blockchains.

papers.title: Impossibility of No-Regret in Multi-Agent Bidding
papers.abstract: We consider $T$ repeated second-price auctions across $n$ pacing bidders with i.i.d. item arrivals, and show that it is computationally impossible for all bidders to achieve no-regret simultaneously while satisfying their respective budget or return-on-investment constraints. Therefore, in the prominent internet auction systems where buyers simultaneously deploy pacing algorithms or automated bidding agents, we cannot hope to achieve joint no-regret guarantees in general. We establish a deterministic relationship that high variance in online bidding systems implies high regret. By showing that one can extract a pacing equilibrium from a low-variance system, we prove PPAD-hardness of attaining joint no-regret. For several widely used bidding algorithms, we also show evidence from dynamical systems and numerical simulations that they can indeed display high-variance behavior through cycling, even on simple market instances.

papers.title: Matrix Samplers and Quantum-Proof Extractors: Their Correspondence and Almost-Optimal Constructions
papers.abstract: We establish an equivalence between matrix samplers and quantum-proof randomness extractors. The classical sampler--extractor equivalence is established by a seminal work of Zuckerman (Random Structures & Algorithms, 1997). Using this equivalence, we construct explicit strong matrix samplers with optimal randomness overhead and near-optimal sample complexity via constructing quantum-proof extractors. Specifically for matrix dimension $D$, accuracy $\varepsilon$ and failure probability $δ\leq\varepsilon$, our matrix sampler uses $m+O_α(\log(D/δ))$ random bits and $O_α(\varepsilon^{-2-α}\log^{1+α}(D/δ))$ samples, for any constant $α>0$. Compared with the matrix sampler of Xun and Zuckerman (CCC 2025), our construction has improvements in two aspects. Under the same optimal random seed length, we can replace the $\operatorname{poly} D$ dependence in the number of samples by $O(\log^{1-γ} D)$. Under the same scale of sample size, we can remove their $\log\log D$ factor in the length of the random seed. Our underlying strong quantum-proof extractor has output length $n-O_α(a+\log(1/η))$ and seed length at most $(1+α)\log a+(2+α)\log(1/η)+O_α(1)$ for $n$-bit sources with conditional min-entropy $n-a$ and error $η$. We also obtain strong quantum-proof extractors for every constant entropy rate, for any error as small as $2^{-Ω(n)}$, having optimal seed length $O(\log(n/η))$ and output length $Ω(n)$, improving previous constructions.

papers.title: Tight Bounds for Randomized Generalized $k$-Server on Uniform Metrics
papers.abstract: In the generalized $k$-server problem, each of $k$ servers moves in its own metric space, and a request $(r_1,\dots,r_k)$ is served once some server $i$ stands at the point $r_i$ of its space. We determine the randomized competitive ratio against an oblivious adversary when every space is a uniform metric. With unit distances the ratio is $Θ(k\log k)$: we give a $(k+1)\ln(2k)$-competitive algorithm and show that for large $k$ every algorithm has ratio at least $\frac{1}{20}k\ln k$, improving the bounds $O(k^2\log k)$ and $Ω(k)$ of Bienkowski, Jeż, and Schmidt. When server $i$ pays $w_i$ per move, the ratio is $\exp(Θ(k))$: we give a $20^k$-competitive algorithm, which also applies to weighted $k$-server on uniform metrics. This improves the $\exp(O(k^2))$ bound of Bijoy, Mondal, and Chiplunkar and matches the $Ω(2^k)$ lower bound of Ayyadevara and Chiplunkar up to the base of the exponent. Both algorithms follow normalized weights exactly, through couplings whose expected movement is controlled by the decrease of the logarithm of the total weight. The lower bound hides a random permutation among the solutions of random permutation constraints, which split into small, well-separated components, and then forbids one position to one server at a time.

papers.title: UPP$^{\text{cc}}$ is Not Closed Under Intersection
papers.abstract: The sign rank of a ${\pm 1}$-valued matrix $A$ is the minimum rank of a real matrix that agrees with $A$ entrywise in sign. For every sufficiently large $d$, we give an explicit matrix $A$ with $2^{Θ(d^2)}$ rows and columns and sign rank $Θ(d)$ such that $A \land A$ has sign rank $2^{Θ(d)}$. Here, $A \land A$ is the communication matrix of the problem obtained by evaluating $A$ on disjoint inputs and taking the conjunction of the results. As the logarithm of sign rank characterizes unbounded-error communication complexity, this implies that the communication class $\mathsf{UPP}^{\mathsf{cc}}$ is not closed under intersection. The starting point for our lower bound is Forster's method, which relates the sign rank of a matrix to the average margin of representations of its rows and columns by points and halfspaces. We study a continuous analog for conjunctions of inner-product sign tests on the unit sphere. Rotational symmetry connects this problem to polynomial sign representations, yielding an exponentially small upper bound on the average margin. This bound holds even when sign constraints are relaxed near the sign tests' decision boundary, allowing us to transfer it to explicit finite sign matrices arising from intersections of integer halfspaces.

papers.title: Game-Theoretic Solvers with Bayesian Opponent Modeling and Moral Rhetoric Framing for GLEE
papers.abstract: We describe the agent we submitted to the GLEE Competition, which plays bargaining, negotiation, and persuasion games against a shared pool of human and AI opponents. The agent is built around three central components: a classical game-theoretic solver to compute numeric moves, an online Bayesian layer to estimate opponent archetypes, and a language model to write accompanying messages. We utilize Rubinstein bargaining for bargaining, Faratin concession for negotiation, and Kamenica--Gentzkow disclosure for persuasion, and adapt those models to live opponents using two separate layers: a Bayesian estimate of the opponent's hidden discount factor, reservation value, or signaling reliability, and a Thompson sampling bandit over five moral-foundation framings coupled with an evidence-intuition spectrum to establish message register. Most of the development effort went into the recurring problem that theoretically optimal policies perform poorly in certain live settings; we report associated failure modes, guardrails we built, and our hypotheses. We additionally evaluate our model over 13,200 Monte Carlo games against 11 synthetic opponent archetypes, an ablation of the opponent-modeling layer, and an extensive analysis of 9,337 live-game messages in which moral rhetoric framing in the persuasion setting is strongly correlated with whether the buyer purchased ($χ^2=616.7$, $p \approx 3.7\times10^{-132}$), surviving controls for quality, round, and configuration.
papers.comment: 13 pages, 1 figure; accepted to 1st Workshop on Interpreting Agent Behavior (IAB) @ NeurIPS 2026

papers.title: Online Interval Selection with Binary Predictions: Optimal Consistency and a Continuous Robustness Tradeoff
papers.abstract: We study online interval selection with binary predictions of membership in a final optimal solution. Requests arrive in arbitrary order; accepted requests may be revoked, but rejected or revoked requests cannot be recovered. With rewards proportional to interval length, the best consistency under finite strict robustness is $d=(3+\sqrt5)/2$ when both guarantees hold almost surely on each fixed input, including for randomized algorithms. A continuous lower bound forces consistency strictly above $d$ at every robustness budget below $4\varphi+3\approx9.472$, whereas our deterministic algorithm attains $d$ with exact robustness $\varphi^5\approx11.090$, where $\varphi=(1+\sqrt5)/2$. Each held interval inherits a ledger recording positive prediction mass lost through irrevocable decisions. A tunable replacement cost gives a continuous family with exact consistency throughout and exact robustness on two parameter intervals, including $(C,R)=(25/9,10)$ and $(4,7)$. Randomization permits expected consistency approaching one with finite expected robustness, whereas almost-sure robustness forces expected consistency strictly above two at every finite budget.
papers.comment: 66 pages, 5 figures. Includes a technical appendix and ancillary evidence tables

papers.title: Optimality and Impossibility in Multidimensional Strategyproof Facility Location
papers.abstract: We study facility location in multidimensional normed spaces with the objective of minimizing social cost, the sum of agents' distances to their nearest facility. A deterministic mechanism selects $k$ facility locations based on the reports of $n$ agents and is strategyproof (SP) if no agent can reduce her distance by misreporting her location. We establish optimal approximation ratios and impossibility results. For a single facility in the Euclidean plane, we prove that the optimal approximation ratios among deterministic SP mechanisms are exactly those obtained by Goel and Hann-Caruthers [SCW 2023] for the coordinate-wise median (CM): $\frac{\sqrt{2(n^2+1)}}{n+1}$ for odd $n\ge3$ and $\sqrt{2}$ for even $n\ge4$. We remove the anonymity assumption from their optimality result. However, CM is not always optimal in non-Euclidean spaces: we give an SP mechanism that minimizes social cost exactly in $\ell_\infty^d$, whereas CM has a tight uniform approximation ratio of $2$ already in the plane. We then consider two facilities in $\ell_p$ spaces with $1<p<\infty$ and prove two impossibility results for every $n>2$. In the plane, no deterministic SP mechanism has a finite approximation ratio. In higher dimensions, the same impossibility holds for anonymous deterministic SP mechanisms. Finally, a reduction using distant agents and a limiting argument extends both impossibility results to every $k>2$ with $n>k$.

papers.title: Differentially Private Preconditioned Power Iteration Method for Principal Component Analysis that Adapts to the Coherence
papers.abstract: In Principal Component Analysis (PCA), we are given as input a matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ and an integer $k\leq d$, and the goal is to find the top $k$ right-singular vectors of $A$. We consider the setting where each row of $A$ is the private data of an individual, and we design an $(ε,δ)$-differentially private algorithm whose utility guarantee improves with the coherence of the input matrix. Prior works were either restricted to the case $k=1$ or ensured significantly weaker privacy protections. Our algorithm is based on a preconditioned variant of the power iteration method that is designed to significantly reduce the noise needed to ensure privacy.

papers.title: Characterizing Maximum Nash Welfare: Envy-Freeness and Proportionality
papers.abstract: When allocating indivisible goods, the maximum Nash welfare rule is known to be the unique welfarist rule satisfying envy-freeness up to one good. We strengthen this characterization by showing that envy-freeness up to one good can be replaced by substantially weaker fairness requirements: envy-freeness up to $k$ goods or proportionality up to $k$ goods, for any fixed $k$. Our characterization holds even for profiles with identical goods.

notes: Warut Suksompong has 3 papers across the five conferences

papers.title: Polynomial-Time Solvability of the Mixed Evacuation Problem
papers.abstract: The mixed evacuation problem is a variant of the dynamic transshipment problem where there exist two modes of transportation and we allocate supplies to each mode of transportation in such a way that we can send all the supplies from sources to sinks within a given time limit. It is known that this problem can be solved in polynomial time when the number of sources and sinks is small. In this paper, we prove that the mixed evacuation problem can be solved in polynomial time with the ellipsoid method.

papers.title: PDE-Based Bounds on Optimal Exponents in Active Simple Hypothesis Testing
papers.abstract: We present general upper and lower bounds on the optimal error exponent for the Active Simple Hypothesis Testing (ASHT) problem. ASHT has been extensively studied across diverse fields including Information Theory, Bandits, and Operations Research, a precise characterization of this optimal exponent has remained elusive. This work combines a recent Partial Differential Equation (PDE) characterization of the optimal exponent by Vijayan (2025) with the comparison principle of viscosity solutions of Hamilton-Jacobi PDEs. This leads to bounds that are parametrized by convex functions, sets and lower Hamiltonian relaxations, a flexibility that generalizes many known results in the literature.

papers.title: Classical Verification of Quantum Computation Beyond the Polynomial Hierarchy
papers.abstract: It is not known whether a classical polynomial-time verifier can verify arbitrary polynomial-time quantum computations with an efficient quantum honest prover without computational assumptions. We show that, relative to a classical oracle, such verification is possible for a language beyond the polynomial hierarchy that is decided exactly in quantum polynomial time. The protocol is public-coin, with perfect completeness and soundness error at most 1/4. To our knowledge, no language with such a proof system was previously proved to lie outside AM relative to an oracle. For every unbounded polynomial-time computable function, the oracle can be chosen so that the message count and the oracle query counts of the quantum algorithm, verifier, and honest prover are bounded by this function of the input length. The message count is optimal up to a constant factor, since for a suitable oracle every interactive proof system for the language uses at least a constant fraction of the messages of our protocol on infinitely many lengths, with a constant depending on its verifier. The language is a variant of recursive Fourier sampling in which code tables encode secrets that address data tables. The tables are evaluated recursively, and the oracle stores only the leaves. The quantum algorithm recovers every secret exactly, and the verifier checks the prover's secrets recursively against random code entries. The recursion restricts the input in a correlated way, as the same secret fixes the code bits and chooses the free coordinate, so Håstad's switching lemma does not apply. We prove a switching theorem for these restrictions, which may be of independent interest. For instances of sufficient height, no constant-depth circuit of size $2^{\mathrm{poly}(n)}$ changes its output with probability above $2^{-Ω(n)}$ when the answer of a random instance is flipped by changing a single leaf.

papers.title: Decomposing Directed Graphs into Partial Orders is Hard
papers.abstract: Comparability graphs represent partial orders and provide natural building blocks for representing a graph as a union of simpler graphs. The analogous task in the directed setting is to represent a digraph as a union of partial orders. Aboulker et al. [arXiv, 2026] recently introduced the partial order decomposition number as a useful structural parameter in their study of tournaments. Formally, a partial order decomposition of a digraph $D$ is a cover of its arc set by transitive acyclic subdigraphs, each representing a strict partial order on the vertex set of $D$. The partial order decomposition number is the minimum number of such subdigraphs needed. We also consider the partitioning variant, in which every arc belongs to exactly one of the partial orders in the decomposition. We prove that, for every fixed $k\geq 2$, deciding whether a digraph admits a decomposition into at most $k$ partial orders is NP-complete, even for directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). For $k=2$, we reduce from NAE-3-SAT. For $k\geq 3$, we reduce from $k$-Coloring, and the reduction yields DAGs with triangle-free underlying graphs. Both reductions establish hardness for both variants. We further show that the minimum cover size and the minimum partition size can differ even on DAGs.

papers.title: Upper and Lower Bounds on the Complexity of Unit-Distance Graph Realization in $\mathbb{Z}^d$
papers.abstract: It is known that the problem of recognizing the existence of a unit-distance realization in $\mathbb{Z}^d$ for a graph $G$ is NP-complete. Here, assuming ETH, we give a sub-exponential lower bound of $2^{Ω(\sqrt{n})}$ for this problem in $\mathbb{Z}^2$ and $2^{Ω(n^{2/3})}$ in $\mathbb{Z}^3$, and give an upper bound of $2^{O(n^{(d-1)/d} (\log n)^2)}$ for the time complexity with an explicit divide-and-conquer algorithm. This approach beats naive exhaustive search by a factor of $\tildeΩ(n^{1/d})$ in the exponent. For 2 and 3 dimensions, our upper and lower bounds match to within a logarithmic factor.

papers.title: When do token systems stabilize? Compatibility constraints and community structure
papers.abstract: Token systems support repeated service exchange without monetary transfers, but their viability depends on the stability of token balances. We study token systems with compatibility constraints among agents. A requester is randomly sampled in each period, and only a few randomly sampled agents are available to provide service. We establish a necessary and sufficient condition for stability and show that the minimum-token rule, which selects the available provider with the lowest token balance, achieves the optimal stability region. We then apply this stability criterion to a random token system generated from stochastic block models with uniformly sampled requesters. We tightly characterize the stability regime by identifying two obstructions to stability: insufficient service opportunities for a group of communities or for an individual agent.

papers.title: Noise Shapes the Surplus: Strategic Play Against No-Regret Learners
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that, in zero-sum games, an optimizer can extract $Ω(\sqrt{T})$ strategic surplus---cumulative payoff above the minimax benchmark---against noiseless no-regret learners with a constant step size. However, in practice, learners often act on perturbed payoff scores and use decaying learning rates $η_t$. Since existing extraction mechanisms rely on exact scores, a natural question is whether noise shields the learner from exploitation and eliminates surplus altogether. We address this question for the widely used class of Follow-the-Regularized-Leader (FTRL) algorithms. Under standard regularity conditions, we establish three results, none of which assumes independence of the noise. First, under summability conditions, passive play of a strategy fixed independently of the horizon earns at most constant surplus. Second, we design a new mechanism that exploits the learner's noise-dependent response: a clairvoyant optimizer who knows the update rule and the limiting mean response secures $Ω(1/η_T)$ surplus whenever that mean is profitable. Third, even when that mean is not profitable, active alternating play extracts $Ω(\sum_{t<T}η_t)$ surplus by exploiting the learner's movement rather than its location, under suitable responsiveness and stability conditions. Finally, at the canonical learning rate $η_t\propto t^{-1/2}$, we recover the noiseless $Ω(\sqrt{T})$ rate for mean-zero, finite-variance perturbations---whether fresh with arbitrary temporal dependence or accumulated from i.i.d. increments---provided the limiting mean response is profitable.

papers.title: Code uniqueness of 4-cell connected disjoint clusters in spatial chromatic model
papers.abstract: The spatial chromatic model (SCM) is a novel entity-oriented spatial data model proposed in recent years. Spatial tessellations formed by SCM have been applied in preliminary analyses of spatial point pattern recognition,spatial topology, and Voronoi diagram generation. Unlike previous spatial tessellation models, a key feature of SCM is that each subspace (cell) possesses a chromatic code, which serves as the foundation for various theoretical analyses and applications of SCM. The uniqueness of cell cluster codes in SCM constitutes an important property of the model. Previous studies have demonstrated the uniqueness of the chromatic codes of 2-cell and 3-cell connected disjoint clusters. Building on this analysis of connected cluster code characteristics, this paper proves the uniqueness of the chromatic codes of 4-cell connected disjoint clusters. The proof results and the new concepts introduced in this study help further refine the spatial chromatic model and provide a theoretical foundation for its subsequent applications.

papers.title: Irreducibility Testing of Sparse Polynomials over Integers is NP-hard and Probabilistic Polynomial Time
papers.abstract: In this paper, we prove that irreducibility testing for sparse polynomials in $\mathbb{Z}[X]$ is coNP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions. That is, there exists no polynomial-time irreducibility test algorithm unless $\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}$. We also provide an upper bound for this problem by demonstrating that the same irreducibility testing problem lies in $\mathsf{PP}\subseteq\mathsf{PSPACE}$; in other words, it can be solved in probabilistic polynomial time and, moreover, within polynomial space. The fact that $\mathsf{SparseIrred}_{\mathbb{Z}}\in\mathsf{PP}$ relies on the quasi-Riemann hypothesis result of Cureton--Thorner and on the uniform effective prime-ideal bound by Frei--Sofos--Widmer just posted recently.

papers.title: Linear-Time FPT Rectilinear Planarity Testing of Series-Parallel Graphs
papers.abstract: A planar graph is rectilinear planar if it admits a planar orthogonal drawing without bends. For series-parallel graphs in the variable embedding setting the best known testing algorithm takes $O(n^2)$ time. We show that rectilinear planarity of a series-parallel graph with maximum degree four can be tested in $2^{O(k)}\cdot n$ time, where $k$ is the number of degree-4 vertices; the planar embedding is not fixed. In particular, the running time is subquadratic when $k=o(\log n)$. Each node of the SPQ$^*$-tree stores the set of its admissible spiralities; we show that this set is a union of $2^{O(k)}$ arithmetic progressions of step two. All proofs are in the paper and are additionally verified in Lean 4 with Mathlib.

papers.title: Approximate Counting for Mixed $p$-Spin Glasses in Weak External Fields via Cluster Expansion
papers.abstract: We give algorithms for approximating the partition function $Z_N$ of the Sherrington--Kirkpatrick (SK) model and finite mixed Ising $p$-spin models with $p\ge 3$. The algorithms apply at a fixed margin below the second-moment threshold $β_{\mathrm f}$ with homogeneous weak external fields $|h|\leqρ_0N^{-1/4}$, for fixed $ρ_0>0$. For any accuracy $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ and failure parameter $δ\in(0,1)$, they approximate $\log Z_N$ to additive error $\varepsilon$. The number of exact operations is polynomial jointly in $N$, $\varepsilon^{-1}$, and $δ^{-1}$. The disorder variables have i.i.d symmetric distribution with unit variance. The failure probability is at most $δ$ plus an explicit disorder tail bound. This tail bound tends to zero under a finite fourth moment condition. Our approach builds on the cluster expansions of Aizenman--Lebowitz--Ruelle~\cite{ALR87} and Dey--Wu~\cites{DW23,DW26}. For higher-order mixtures, we retain hypergraphs using few vertices and evaluate their total weight deterministically through local spin averages and inclusion--exclusion. For SK, we impose cutoffs on the number of vertices of degree at least three and on the total number of edges. We estimate the retained sum using randomized color coding~\cite{AYZ95}. A lower tail control based on reverse hypercontractivity~\cite{MOS13} converts the mean-square approximation of the normalized partition function into logarithmic accuracy.
papers.comment: 38 pages, 3 figures. AI-assisted and a companion lean formalization in https://github.com/qiangwu2/approximate-counting-spin-glasses

papers.title: Strategyproof Deep Reinforcement Learning for Online Resource Allocation
papers.abstract: Online resource allocation faces two coupled challenges: (1) allocating scarce resources efficiently under uncertain future demand, and (2) ensuring that agents report task valuations and requirements truthfully (strategyproofness). Reinforcement Learning (RL) adapts allocation decisions through experience but does not necessarily ensure strategyproofness. Existing strategyproof RL uses a linear allocation rule, which limits the resource interactions it can represent. Neural mechanism design methods offer greater expressiveness, but provide only approximate incentive guarantees. Against this background, we introduce the first strategyproof deep RL mechanism for online resource allocation. It integrates three novel components: (i) a monotonic neural network that learns nonlinear interactions by construction (higher reported value cannot reduce acceptance, while a longer reported duration or larger resource requirement cannot increase it); (ii) a generalised critical payment: the lowest accepted value, with all other inputs fixed; and (iii) training by either RL or imitation of an existing rule. Together, monotonicity and the critical payment ensure strategyproofness and individual rationality, while the neural rule provides flexibility and imitation improves training efficiency. Empirically, on a four-resource stream with two partner pairs that a linear difference cannot represent, the neural rule achieves 97.8% of an offline welfare upper bound, compared with 93.8% for a linear learner and 89.0% for first-come, first-served, closing 65% and 80% of the remaining optimality gap, respectively. Moreover, imitation reaches 97.5% in only 261 seconds, about 89 times faster than RL.

papers.title: A Linear Kernel for Planar Semitotal Domination
papers.abstract: A set of vertices $S$ in a graph $G$ is a semitotal dominating set if $S$ is a dominating set and every vertex in $S$ has a witness, that is, another vertex in $S$ within distance at most two. The Semitotal Domination problem asks whether $G$ admits such a set of size at most $k$. We study this problem parameterized by the solution size. We provide a linear kernel of size $358k$ on planar graphs, a result that adds to several existing linear kernels for other domination variants on planar graphs. Additionally, we show Semitotal Domination is $W[2]$-hard on split graphs, on bipartite graphs and on $t$-claw-free graphs, it is $W[1]$-hard on circle graphs.

papers.title: Conservative Policy Iteration For Zero-Sum POSGs
papers.abstract: Occupancy-state reductions make dynamic programming possible for zero-sum partially observable stochastic games (zs-POSGs). Existing point-based solvers usually optimise a central value function. This restores Bellman recursion, but it requires point-based updates over high-dimensional occupancy spaces. We introduce an approximate policy-iteration algorithm for finite-horizon zs-POSGs. The method maintains one policy per player and updates both jointly along occupancy trajectories induced by conservative policy updates. Instead of approximating a full central value function, each update uses a single supporting hyperplane induced by the current joint policy. The algorithm alternates local policy improvements, conservative updates, and persistent exploration. Computation is therefore concentrated on occupancy regions where the current joint policy is exploitable. On finite-horizon zero-sum POSG benchmarks, the method is competitive at small horizons and often improves the runtime-exploitability trade-off at larger horizons compared with PBVI, HSVI, and CFR+.

papers.title: On surfaces, that fill the space
papers.abstract: The article is devoted to the construction of dimension-raising maps of cubes with the highest possible Holder exponent. In particular, a square-to-cube mapping with a Holder exponent of $2/3$ is constructed, which is a solution to the V.I.Arnold problem.
